extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York / American electorate considering ratification of the Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A set of normative principles and practical criteria arguing why the proposed national Constitution is necessary and superior to the existing Confederation, aimed at persuading citizens to support ratification. Emphasizes enforceability, division of powers, and the practical means of securing union, credit, and respect abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: Union is essential to the political safety and happiness of the people; severing the Union would expose the nation to ambition, avarice, jealousy, misrepresentation, and national humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton stresses that preservation of the Union prevents a catalogue of public misfortunes: breaches of engagements, unpaid debts, loss of posts, inability to repel aggression, exclusion from navigation (Mississippi), collapse of public credit and commerce, and loss of respect abroad. Appeal to these concrete harms is used to justify constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing Confederation contains material imperfections and fundamental errors which prevent it from rescuing the nation from impending anarchy and national humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay enumerates concrete failures under the Confederation (no troops, no treasury, inability to enforce treaties, depressed land values, declining commerce). These examples are offered as evidence that mere admission of defects is insufficient unless remedies granting necessary powers are adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Great Vice: LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS (not individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A core defect is the principle of legislation for States or Governments in their corporate capacities, as contradistinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When laws address only political bodies rather than persons, they become recommendations states may obey or disregard. This principle produces capricious noncompliance, making the Confederation impotent and inviting either civil war or dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be attended with a sanction/enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to the idea of a law that it be attended with a sanction — a penalty or punishment for disobedience — enforceable either by courts (magistracy) or, failing that, by military force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton argues enforcement through ordinary courts (addressing individuals) is the legitimate and practical instrument; if enforcement requires military coercion against States, government degenerates into force and is not true civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend the authority of the Union to the persons of the citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government must have authority over individual citizens (the proper objects of government), not be limited to issuing directives to state governments as corporate entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Union should be empowered to employ ordinary magistrates and the courts to execute its resolutions directly upon individuals, thereby preventing evasions by state legislatures and ensuring measures take immediate effect without state intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on military coercion for ordinary enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution that can only be kept in motion by a large standing army to execute ordinary requisitions would degenerate into military despotism and is impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes the Union lacks resources to maintain such an army and historical confederacies that relied on force failed; relying on arms to coerce states would either be ineffective or lead to civil war and dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vest national authority over commerce, finance, negotiation, and war
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers over commerce, public finance, negotiation (diplomacy), and war are proper objects for the national government and should be lodged in the national depository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These central, externally-facing functions attract ambition and require uniform national management; domestic police, agriculture, and other local concerns should remain with state governments as they are inappropriate for general jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve state control of ordinary criminal and civil justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice by State governments is the most powerful and universal source of popular obedience and attachment and will serve as a counterpoise to national power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because local courts directly affect everyday life, they secure citizen loyalty to state governments; this localized influence makes states natural rivals or checks on the national government and explains why national powers should focus on broader concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution of national measures must not depend on concurrence of many sovereign wills
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Confederation the concurrence of thirteen distinct sovereign wills is required to execute important measures, making effective national action impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton explains how partial compliance, self-interest, and the temptation to free-ride produce progressive withdrawal of support until the national government's wheels stop; a workable constitution must avoid requiring unanimous or multi-sovereign concurrence for ordinary enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design government consistent with human nature and factional tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because passions, faction, and self-interest move men, government must be constituted so it can control these tendencies through enforceable laws and institutions rather than relying on republican virtue alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton invokes human nature to argue that diffuse decision-making and divided authority invite faction and noncompliance; therefore institutional mechanisms (courts, direct authority over individuals, appropriate allocation of powers) are necessary for stability.
